item.content:encoded:
News / NewsBTC / Binance Hack: US Moves to Recover $1.1 Billion, but Who Gets the Money?

Binance Hack: US Moves to Recover $1.1 Billion, but Who Gets the Money? 5 min read

USDCUSD BNBUSD Key takeaways US authorities filed a civil forfeiture complaint on November 23 seeking more than $1.1 billion in USDC linked to the October 29 Binance hack, across 36 addresses on 18 blockchains. Circle froze the funds but says it cannot technically move them, so it proposes issuing replacement USDC to the US after a forfeiture order. Frozen is not recovered: the filings advance the legal-control stage, while final distribution and ownership remain undecided. A separate Abu Dhabi court order adds a second jurisdiction, and Circle’s reserve and supply reporting for the replacement tokens will deserve scrutiny. Nearly four weeks after the Binance hack, US authorities have filed a civil forfeiture complaint seeking more than $1.1 billion in USDC linked to the October theft. The money is already subject to restrictions, but the latest court filings reveal a complication: freezing stolen cryptocurrency is considerably easier than returning it. The complaint, filed on November 23, in the US District Court for the District of Columbia, targets USDC associated with 36 cryptocurrency addresses across 18 blockchains.

Federal investigators attribute the October 29 attack to North Korean hacking groups, including the Lazarus Group. The complaint puts the value of the original theft at approximately $6 billion. For Binance, the latest legal action represents another opportunity to recover a portion of its losses. For the wider cryptocurrency industry, however, the case raises questions about the authority stablecoin issuers exercise over digital assets and what happens when governments become involved. Binance Hack Recovery Enters a New Legal Phase The assets targeted by US authorities are not an entirely new discovery. Earlier this month, NewsBTC reported that Circle had frozen approximately $1.1 billion in USDC linked to the Binance hack, following cooperation with law enforcement. What has changed is the government’s attempt to establish a legal basis for taking possession of those assets. According to the court documents, US authorities obtained a temporary restraining order on November 12. Prosecutors subsequently requested that the restrictions remain in place throughout the civil forfeiture proceedings. Both Binance and Circle consented to the initial restraining order and the requested extension, according to the government’s November 23 application. The agreement between the companies and federal authorities reduces one immediate obstacle to preserving the funds. It does not, however, resolve the question of their ultimate ownership or distribution. Civil forfeiture proceedings are directed against property believed to be connected to criminal activity. Interested parties can assert legitimate claims to that property through the legal process. In this case, prosecutors are seeking forfeiture of the assets to the United States. That is not the same thing as a court ordering their immediate return to Binance. Circle Cannot Simply Send the Frozen USDC Back Perhaps the most interesting disclosure in the complaint concerns Circle itself. The stablecoin issuer can restrict transfers involving USDC held at particular blockchain addresses. However, that authority does not necessarily give Circle direct control over the wallets holding those tokens. The complaint states that Circle: “ does not have the technical ability to transfer the Defendant Property from the blocklisted Subject Addresses to the United States US forfeiture complaint · November 23 filing Instead, Circle has agreed to issue an equivalent amount of replacement USDC and transfer those tokens to US authorities upon receiving a forfeiture order from the court. The proposed arrangement exposes an unusual feature of centralized stablecoins. An issuer can prevent tokens from circulating without possessing the private keys needed to move them. It also raises an accounting question that deserves attention. If replacement tokens are issued, what ultimately happens to the original frozen USDC, and how will Circle ensure that the treatment of those balances is reflected accurately in its outstanding supply and reserve reporting? The issuance of replacement tokens would not, by itself, prove that USDC had become undercollateralized. Nevertheless, transparency around the implementation would be important for a stablecoin whose credibility depends on confidence in its backing. The immediate concern is not whether Circle can create new tokens. It is whether the entire recovery process can be independently accounted for. The $1.1 Billion Is Not Back With Binance Yet The temptation to describe the Justice Department’s announcement as a billion-dollar recovery is understandable. It is also premature. There are three separate stages involved: restricting access to the stolen assets, obtaining legal authority over them and determining how they will ultimately be distributed. The November 23 filings advance the second stage. They do not establish that the third has been completed. The $1.1 billion Binance recovery process. Source: US District Court for the District of Columbia filings, November 23, 2026. There is also a cross-border complication. On November 18, Reuters reported that an Abu Dhabi court had directed several cryptocurrency companies, including Circle, to preserve digital assets associated with the Binance theft. The involvement of authorities in both the United States and the United Arab Emirates illustrates how a single cryptocurrency theft can generate legal proceedings across multiple jurisdictions. Blockchain transactions may cross national borders without much difficulty. Establishing ownership rights over the assets involved is a considerably less straightforward exercise. That does not mean the US and UAE proceedings are necessarily in conflict. But the ultimate disposition of the funds will require more than an announcement from either government. For investors assessing Binance’s financial position, the distinction between frozen assets and recovered capital is particularly important. Restricted cryptocurrency should not automatically be treated as money already returned to the exchange. The Binance Hack Tests the Case for Centralized Stablecoins For years, the ability of stablecoin issuers to freeze tokens has been criticized by advocates of decentralized finance. The Binance case demonstrates the other side of that argument. Without Circle’s ability to restrict transactions, preserving such a large amount of cryptocurrency for potential recovery would have been more difficult. In this particular case, centralized control has provided a mechanism that may help prevent suspected criminals from benefiting from stolen assets. The uncomfortable question is whether the cryptocurrency industry can benefit from that authority while also demanding meaningful safeguards against its misuse. The answer depends partly on transparency. Token holders should be able to understand why assets were frozen, under what legal authority restrictions remain in place and how disputes over ownership are resolved. The same standard should apply to the exchange, the stablecoin issuer and the government. The next significant development in the Binance case will be the court’s treatment of the forfeiture claim and any competing claims to the assets. Circle’s proposed issuance of replacement USDC will also deserve scrutiny if it proceeds. Until then, the $1.1 billion should be understood as assets subject to an ongoing recovery effort, not a completed repayment. For a cryptocurrency industry that frequently celebrates the speed of moving money, the Binance hack is a reminder that getting it back can be an entirely different business.

pangolin.exchange @pangolindex

Two dates. One to deploy. One for everyone. 🔺 🛠ï¸ November 26 - Mainnet deployment 🌎 December 10 - Open to everyone Pangolin ve(3,3) is coming. Lock. Vote. Earn. pic.twitter.com/Kyzy5dQjbi

PNG Info Pangolin is a multichain decentralized exchange (DEX) operating on the Avalanche Network, designed to provide users with advanced tooling, deep liquidity, and an easy onboarding process for a seamless trading experience. The platform facilitates cryptocurrency swaps by leveraging the capabilities of the Avalanche Network to ensure fast and secure transactions. Pangolin aims to enhance user experience by offering intuitive interfaces and features that simplify the trading process for both new and experienced traders. PNG is the native governance token of Pangolin, granting community members the power to influence the platform’s development. It adheres to a 100% community-focused distribution model, ensuring that all tokens are allocated directly to users with no reserves for advisors, investors, or insiders. This model promotes a decentralized and community-driven approach to the platform’s growth and governance.

Enjin Coin to Hold Misfit Galaxy Game Night on November 25th 1 min read

Enjin Coin will host a Misfit Galaxy community game session on Discord on November 25th at 17:00 UTC. Participants will have a chance to win NFTs infused with ENJ. Refer to the official tweet by ENJ:

Enjin @enjin

Misfit Galaxy Game Night confirmed! Come hang out and play @misfitgalaxymmo with the Enjin community this Wednesday! 📅 Wednesday, November 25 🕛 17:00 UTC 📍 https://t.co/OFudFl68b8 ENJ infused NFTs will be up for grabs 👀 See you in the galaxy! pic.twitter.com/oULzQYeFVM

Nov 23, 2026

ENJ Info Enjin is a comprehensive platform designed around the intersection of blockchain and gaming. Spearheaded by Enjin, this ecosystem offers a suite of interconnected gaming products with the Enjin Network at its core, where users engage in social gaming activities, including the creation of gaming websites, clans, chat forums, and virtual item storefronts. Central to Enjin’s functionality is its ability to let developers tokenize in-game items on the Ethereum blockchain. Through this mechanism, real-world value is imparted to these digital assets, enabling their purchase, sale, and trade on integrated marketplaces. This digitization process does more than just virtualize items; it brings transparency, verifies authenticity, and guarantees the scarcity of the tokenized assets, enhancing their inherent value and utility across various applications. Serving as the backbone of the Enjin ecosystem is the Enjin Coin (ENJ), an ERC-20 token. This digital store of value is integral to the creation and backing of blockchain assets, especially non-fungible tokens (NFTs). Every NFT produced within the Enjin platform has ENJ embedded within it, effectively locking this value and removing the corresponding ENJ from the general circulation. This system not only ensures that the assets possess inherent value but also provides liquidity and introduces an anti-inflationary model. Furthermore, Enjin’s distinctive “melting” feature grants users the option to dissolve their assets, subsequently reclaiming the intrinsic ENJ.

TRON DAO @trondao

Explore blockchain with TRON Academy and @ucblockchain . 🎓 Join our virtual workshop covering TRON, stablecoin use cases, and the @JustinSunPrize . 📅 December 2 🕐 5 PM CST / 6 PM EST Request to join 👇 https://t.co/xQpBHQl8XK pic.twitter.com/EOV1N65oD5

TRX Info Tron (TRX) is a blockchain project designed to enable the creation of decentralized applications (dApps). Originally built on the Ethereum blockchain in 2017, Tron later migrated to its own network protocol. The Tron network offers high throughput and scalability, making it suitable for applications with a high volume of transactions, such as gaming and social media platforms. One of the unique features of Tron is its three-layer architecture, consisting of the storage layer, the core protocol layer, and the application layer. This architecture provides great flexibility for developers and allows the creation of complex and functional applications. The TRX token serves as the primary asset within the Tron network and is used to manage network resources, participate in voting, pay fees, and earn rewards through staking.

Nov 24, 2026

HBAR Info Hedera (HBAR) is a decentralized public network that allows individuals and businesses to create powerful decentralized applications (dApps). Its native cryptocurrency is HBAR, used to power decentralized applications, build peer-to-peer payment and micropayment business models, and protect the network from malicious actors. Hedera stands out from other blockchain technologies due to its use of hashgraph consensus, which promises the benefits of blockchain – decentralization, distribution, and security through hashing – with enhanced speed, efficiency, and scalability. This technology enables Hedera to process thousands of transactions per second in contrast to traditional blockchains, making it an appealing option for enterprise use cases.
